chunks: ISRs at the hardware and software level. The question: Describe how ISRs work at the hardware and software levels.
When an interrupt fires, hardware and software share the work. On an Arm Cortex-M chip, the hardware automatically saves eight registers onto the stack.
It then fetches the handler's address and jumps there. Because of this, the handler can be an ordinary function written in C, a common programming language.
The handler's job is short: read the data, clear the event's flag bit, and update shared variables. Returning triggers the hardware to restore everything and resume.
Picture hot-desking. Before a colleague borrows your desk, a porter automatically boxes up the papers you use most and notes the page you were on.
If the colleague needs any other drawer, he tidies it back himself before leaving. Then the porter unpacks the box, and you carry on as if nothing happened.
The porter is the hardware. The colleague's own tidying is extra code the compiler adds.
The 8-word frame is pushed by hardware, growing the stack by 32 bytes before the first ISR instruction runs.
Anything the compiler adds (R4-R11 and local variables) goes below it, so a nest of k ISRs costs at least 32k bytes.
Register: a tiny, fast storage cell inside the processor that holds values being worked on.
Stack frame: the saved state the hardware pushes onto the stack, a memory area used as scratch space. On Cortex-M that is 8 values, 32 bytes.
Compiler: the program that turns C code into the processor's instructions.
Magic return value: a special value, EXC RETURN, that tells the hardware "this is an interrupt return, so restore the saved state".
At 72 megahertz, entry takes about 12 cycles, so 12 over 72 megahertz about 167 nanoseconds. The handler reads a received serial byte, which also clears the flag.
The return takes about 12 more cycles. That is 24 cycles, or about 0. 33 microseconds of overhead per interrupt.
At 50,000 interrupts per second, the overhead alone is 24 over 72 megahertz times 50 000 about 1. 7 % of the processor.
On a small 8-bit AVR chip, the compiler's code does most of the saving, so the same job costs about 34 cycles. That is the whole idea.

"In hardware, the NVIC picks the interrupt, the core finishes its instruction, pushes eight registers onto the stack, reads the handler address from the vector table and switches to handler mode, about 12 cycles on a Cortex-M.
Because the caller-saved registers are already saved, the ISR is a plain C function: it reads the data, clears the flag and touches volatile shared variables.
Returning with the special EXC RETURN value makes the hardware pop the frame and resume. On AVR the software prologue does more of this."
